angle: Do LSTM / deep hydrologic models beat gradient-boosted trees for ungauged basins at small n
verdict: DO NOT PURSUE an LSTM/deep-sequence pivot. The angle is answered decisively in the negative, and the strongest evidence for that answer is verified. (1) The required head-to-head does not exist: across every source examined, NO study anywhere compares an LSTM against XGBoost/random forest/any gradient-boosted tree for a water-quality CONCENTRATION target under a spatial holdout. There is no published result that could justify the switch, at any n. (2) The one verified paper that runs the right experiment on the right target -- Pandit et al. 2025 (WRR, doi:10.1029/2024WR039207), an LSTM trained on CONUS-wide high-frequency nitrate sensors -- fails in exactly the way this project already fails: median KGE 0.60 under temporal validation collapses to 0.34 under spatial validation within the Mississippi River Basin (0.18 CONUS-wide). A well-resourced EPA/academic team with continental training data and a deep sequence model still cannot recover the absolute between-site level of nitrate at unmonitored basins. That is external, independent confirmation that 'good timer, mediocre site-ranker' is a property of the ungauged-nitrate PROBLEM, not a defect of gradient-boosted trees. (3) The verified deep-learning scaling evidence points the wrong way for n=19: Gauch/Kratzert et al. 2024 (HESS Opinions 28:4187) find median NSE still rising monotonically at 531 CAMELS basins with no plateau ('even these 531 basins are most likely not to be enough'), and find that training on HUC-sized subsets of 2-79 basins -- the scale of our 19 families -- is WORSE than pooling everything. Our effective sample sits far down the left tail of a curve that had not flattened at 28x our size. (4) Every LSTM number in the literature that looks good is either streamflow (not water quality), temporally held out (not spatial), benchmarked only against process-based models (never against trees), or dependent on inputs we do not have at an ungauged pin (discharge, local nitrate history). THE ANGLE'S REAL PAYOFF IS NOT ARCHITECTURAL. The single most actionable item recovered here is the Pandit Shapley result naming TILE DRAINAGE, roadway density, and wetland cover as the dominant SPATIAL drivers of MEAN nitrate concentration -- all three absent from the current 68-feature set, and tile drainage being the control the project already flagged as dominant-but-missing with no identified source. Pandit et al. operationalized a CONUS tile-drainage layer, which means a usable one exists; AgTile-US (30 m, CONUS, free, Figshare) is the leading candidate and should be verified against the paper's data-availability statement once the PMC embargo lifts 2026-08-09. Redirect this angle's budget from architecture to static between-site attributes.

findings.claim: An LSTM trained on CONUS-wide high-frequency nitrate sensor data does NOT solve ungauged-basin nitrate concentration, and fails in the same mode as this project: timing preserved, absolute level lost. Pandit, Golden, Christensen, Lane & Husic (2025), 'Deep Learning Prediction and Interpretation of Riverine Nitrate Export Across the Mississippi River Basin,' WRR 61(8) e2024WR039207, report median KGE = 0.60 under temporal validation (unseen periods at sites included in training) versus median KGE = 0.18 under spatial validation, which the authors define verbatim as 'prediction in unmonitored basins.' Restricted to the Mississippi River Basin -- which contains Iowa and is the paper's featured region -- spatial-validation median KGE = 0.34. USE 0.34, NOT 0.18, for any Iowa-facing argument: the region-matched degradation is 0.60 -> 0.34 (drop 0.26), not 0.60 -> 0.18 (drop 0.42). Citing 0.18 overstates the collapse by roughly 60%, because the CONUS figure is depressed by arid/mountainous regions with almost no nitrate sensors and that we will never serve. The conclusion survives either way -- KGE 0.34 at unmonitored basins is weak, and KGE rewards reproducing a series' mean and variance, which is precisely the between-site level term we fail at.
findings.effectSize: median KGE 0.60 (temporal validation) -> 0.34 (spatial validation, Mississippi River Basin) -> 0.18 (spatial validation, CONUS-wide). Iowa-relevant drop = 0.26 KGE.
findings.splitProtocol: Both reported and explicitly distinguished by the authors: temporal-holdout (0.60) and spatial-holdout / prediction-in-unmonitored-basins (0.18 CONUS, 0.34 MRB). The spatial protocol is the correct protocol class for our deployment target. FOLD CONSTRUCTION UNKNOWN AND NOT LEAK-SAFE-EQUIVALENT: the full text is inaccessible (Wiley HTTP 402; PMC12425153 embargoed until 2026-08-09), and nothing establishes that nested/upstream-downstream sites were forced into the same fold the way our basin-family CV does. Treat as 'spatial-holdout, fold construction unknown.'
findings.nBasins: UNVERIFIED. The abstract says only 'high-frequency sensor data from across the conterminous US' and gives no site count. Figures of 95 and 148 circulate in the extracted corpus but could not be substantiated from any accessible source. The '1980-2022' span that appears alongside them is the MRB hindcast/application period, NOT the LSTM training window -- training used high-frequency sensor data, which is essentially post-2010. Re-verify site counts after 2026-08-09 at https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC12425153/
sources: https://agupubs.onlinelibrary.wiley.com/doi/10.1029/2024WR039207 (doi:10.1029/2024WR039207, WRR 61(8) e2024WR039207, 2025-08-09, CC-BY-NC, PMID 40948694, PMCID PMC12425153). Abstract retrieved verbatim and identically via Crossref, OpenAlex, Semantic Scholar Graph API, DOAJ API, NCBI efetch, and Europe PMC.
findings.feasibilityAtN19: NOT FEASIBLE as a method to import. The study's training pool is a continental sensor network spanning many hydroclimates -- plainly far more independent spatial units than our 19 basin families, though the exact count is unverified. An LSTM at our sample size should be expected to underperform the current XGBoost, not rescue it. What IS usable at n=19 is the paper's diagnosis, not its architecture.
findings.worksAtUngaugedPin: The PROTOCOL is the right analogue -- prediction in unmonitored basins requires no target-site observations, exactly our deployment target. But the RESULT is a warning, not a solution: state-of-the-art deep learning at continental scale still transfers poorly to unmonitored basins for nitrate concentration. CAVEAT: the LSTM's input list is not in the abstract, and nitrate-concentration LSTMs of this type commonly ingest DISCHARGE as a dynamic forcing. If so, even the 0.34 was achieved with streamflow information our arbitrary map pin does not have (only 22 of our 85 sites have discharge; zero of the 61 IWQIS sites do).
findings.metricComparabilityWarning: KGE on a continuous daily concentration series is NOT commensurable with our LOFO CLF AUC 0.820 / PR-AUC 0.634 on a binary 10 mg/L exceedance target, nor with our REG R2 0.328 (KGE and R2 are different functionals). There is no arithmetic bridge. This paper bounds only the question 'would an LSTM fix our between-site problem?' It says nothing about whether AUC 0.820 is near a ceiling, and it cannot be used to argue our numbers are good or bad.

findings.claim: THE HIGHEST-VALUE ITEM RECOVERED FROM THIS ENTIRE ANGLE, and it is not architectural. Shapley-value interpretation of the same CONUS nitrate LSTM identified TILE DRAINAGE, ROADWAY DENSITY, and WETLAND COVER as the key spatial drivers influencing MEAN nitrate concentrations, with quantitative non-linear thresholds in their influence. Verbatim from the abstract: 'Interpretable Shapley values identified key spatial drivers influencing mean nitrate concentrations-tile drainage, roadway density, wetland cover-and quantitative, non-linear thresholds in their influence, offering management targets.' These are drivers of the SITE-LEVEL MEAN -- the between-site term that is this project's entire remaining headroom -- and all three are ABSENT from the current 68-feature set. This is independent, primary-source, deep-model-derived confirmation of the project's own diagnosis that the deficit is missing static between-site information, and it names tile drainage first. It also proves that a CONUS- or MRB-extent tile-drainage layer EXISTS and is operationally usable, which directly contradicts the project note that 'NO data source has been identified yet.'
findings.effectSize: Qualitative ranking of top spatial drivers plus unreported threshold values; no per-feature effect size is recoverable while the full text is embargoed. Falsifiable prediction for this project: adding basin-aggregated tile-drainage fraction, wetland fraction, and road density should improve between_r2 / between_rate_r2 specifically, and should NOT move within_r2.
findings.splitProtocol: not-applicable -- interpretation of a fitted model, not a held-out performance number. The model interpreted is the one whose spatial validation gave median KGE 0.34 (MRB).
sources: https://agupubs.onlinelibrary.wiley.com/doi/10.1029/2024WR039207 -- abstract text confirmed verbatim across Crossref, OpenAlex, Semantic Scholar, DOAJ, NCBI efetch, and Europe PMC by three independent verifiers.
findings.feasibilityAtN19: HIGHLY FEASIBLE and the recommended use of this angle's budget. Adding three static basin-aggregated attributes to an existing booster costs 3 features against 19 independent units -- cheap, and it targets the exact term where all headroom lives. It also matches the project's own empirical pattern that the only wins have come from geometry and static geography while every hydrologically-motivated temporal feature has failed.
findings.worksAtUngaugedPin: YES, fully. Tile drainage, wetland cover, and road density are static raster/vector layers computable over any delineated basin from public national products. They require no target-site observations, no gauge, and no monitored upstream neighbor -- they are computed from the NLDI-delineated basin polygon alone, exactly like the existing CDL and N-surplus features.

findings.claim: ABSENCE OF EVIDENCE, ESTABLISHED RATHER THAN ASSUMED: no verified source examined for this angle contains a head-to-head comparison of an LSTM against XGBoost, random forest, or any gradient-boosted tree for a water-quality concentration target under ANY split protocol, let alone a spatial one. Kratzert/Gauch et al. 2024 (HESS Opinions 28:4187-4201) was read in full: its only non-LSTM baselines are the distributed hydrologic model mHM and the macroscale land-surface model VIC; the strings for tree-ensemble methods do not appear. The Pandit et al. 2025 nitrate paper's accessible text contains no tree baseline of any kind -- its interpretability layer is SHAP applied to the deep model, not a competing tree predictor. Consequently, a decision to replace this project's XGBoost with an LSTM CANNOT be justified by citing the PUB literature: the required comparison has not been run by anyone, on any target, at any basin count.
findings.effectSize: No effect size exists. This is a documented absence, and per the standing rule it is reported as absence rather than silently dropped.
sources: https://hess.copernicus.org/articles/28/4187/2024/ (Kratzert, Gauch, Klotz & Nearing 2024, HESS Opinions 28:4187-4201, doi:10.5194/hess-28-4187-2024) -- full text read; zero GBDT and zero water-quality content confirmed.

https://agupubs.onlinelibrary.wiley.com/doi/10.1029/2024WR039207 -- abstract and all open metadata; no RF/XGBoost/gradient-boosting string present. Full text embargoed, so a supplementary benchmark table cannot be formally ruled out.
findings.feasibilityAtN19: not-applicable -- this is a statement about the literature, not a method. Its practical force is that the burden of proof for an LSTM pivot is entirely unmet, and meeting it would require running the experiment ourselves at n=19, where seed variance across 19 held-out families would likely swamp the effect being measured.

findings.claim: THE DEEP-LEARNING SCALING EVIDENCE ARGUES AGAINST AN LSTM AT n=19, USING THE DEEP-LEARNING COMMUNITY'S OWN NUMBERS. Kratzert, Gauch, Klotz & Nearing (2024), HESS Opinions 28:4187-4201, Section 4 'How many basins are necessary?' finds median NSE still rising monotonically with training-set size at the full 531-basin CAMELS pool, with no plateau: 'even these 531 basins are most likely not to be enough to train optimal LSTM models for streamflow.' Section 5 additionally trains on hydrologically informed subsets -- the 18 USGS HUC regions, 'with between 2 and 79 basins per HUC,' i.e. groupings of roughly the size of our 19 independent basin families -- and concludes 'even if enough basins exist to divide your training data into hydrologically informed training sets, one is likely to be better off simply training a single model with all available data.' Our effective sample sits far down the left tail of a curve that had not flattened at 28x our size, in exactly the subset-size regime the authors found to underperform.
findings.effectSize: Direction and monotonicity are stated in text and shown in Fig. 6; the paper reports NO numeric median NSE values anywhere in text, tables, or captions -- the curve is figure-only, so no effect magnitude can be quoted and no minimum-viable basin count is ever stated. Subset comparison in Fig. 7 is reported as direction plus significance, not as an NSE delta.
findings.splitProtocol: temporal-holdout ONLY, and at GAUGED basins -- the weakest possible protocol relative to our LOFO. Main setup: train 1 Oct 1999 - 30 Sep 2008, test 1 Oct 1989 - 30 Sep 1999. The Fig. 6 sample-size experiment uses 'k-fold cross-validation so that all models were tested on the same basin(s) where they were trained (during different time periods).' There is NO ungauged-basin experiment anywhere in the paper; the authors explicitly state 'this analysis does not account for the value of hydrologic diversity for prediction in ungauged basins.' None of its NSE numbers may be placed on the same axis as our LOFO 0.820.
findings.nBasins: 531 CAMELS-US basins for all LSTM experiments; 489 for the mHM/VIC benchmark subset; HUC subsets of 2-79 basins each across 18 HUCs.
sources: https://hess.copernicus.org/articles/28/4187/2024/ -- doi:10.5194/hess-28-4187-2024, article type literally 'HESS Opinions' (a position paper). Full text read and quoted verbatim by verifiers.
findings.feasibilityAtN19: This finding IS the n=19 assessment, and it is negative. The paper's own evidence places any LSTM/EA-LSTM proposal at the extreme low end of a curve the authors describe as not yet asymptotic at 531 basins, and its subset experiment at HUC scale (2-79 basins) is the closest available proxy for our regime -- it lost to full pooling. Anyone citing this paper as support for switching from XGBoost to an LSTM is citing a paper that (a) never tested a GBDT, (b) never touched water quality, (c) never held out a basin spatially, and (d) whose sample-size analysis implies our n is well below where regional LSTMs start to pay off.
findings.worksAtUngaugedPin: NO -- and the paper provides no evidence either way, since it contains no ungauged-basin experiment. The word 'ungauged' appears only as motivating prose. A careless reader searching the text for 'ungauged' could wrongly conclude the paper contains PUB results; it does not.
findings.oneTransferableTakeaway: The pooling argument itself -- train across basins, never on a single one -- which this project already satisfies by construction, and which therefore cannot deliver further gains here. A secondary implication worth noting: if enlarging the basin pool is the operative lever, the escape hatch from n=19 is pulling in out-of-state nitrate monitoring sites across the MRB, not specializing further to Iowa.

findings.claim: THE CONTINENTAL NITRATE LSTM'S REPORTED SKILL IS DRIVEN BY SENSOR-DATA DENSITY, NOT BY ARCHITECTURE -- and this is the authors' own stated conclusion, not an adversarial reading. The EPA Science Inventory record for the companion AGU 2023 presentation (Pandit, Lane, Christensen, Golden & Husic, presented 2023-12-15) reports median R2 and KGE around 0.5 across all sites, exceeding 0.7 in the agricultural Midwest but falling below 0.3 at data-sparse western sites, and states that the work highlights 'the necessity of sensor data for accurate simulations.' Because our deployment target is an arbitrary ungauged Iowa map pin with no nitrate history, the source's own stated mechanism predicts failure at the target regardless of n or architecture. The n=19 constraint is a second, independent objection, not the main one.
findings.effectSize: median R2 and KGE ~0.5 across all sites; >0.7 in the agricultural Midwest; <0.3 in the data-sparse West. These values MUST NOT be placed on the same axis as our LOFO 0.820 / R2 0.328 under any circumstance, because no split protocol is reported.
findings.splitProtocol: NONE REPORTED. This is the decisive limitation of the source.
findings.nBasins: 148 monitoring locations total, with NO stated train/validation partition. The '95 sites' figure that circulates alongside this record does NOT appear in it -- the string is absent -- and appears to have been imported from the later peer-reviewed publication. The defensible ratio to our 19 independent basin families is ~7.8x.
sources: https://cfpub.epa.gov/si/si_public_record_Report.cfm?dirEntryId=360394&Lab=CEMM -- EPA Science Inventory record for an AGU 2023 Fall Meeting PRESENTATION. NOT a paper: a single-paragraph record, no methods section, no DOI, not peer-reviewed.
findings.feasibilityAtN19: The source cannot bear ANY inferential weight about architecture transfer at reduced n, favorable or unfavorable -- there is no methodological content to evaluate. Faulting a conference abstract for 'reporting no basin-count ablation' is trivially true; the sharper objection is that it reports no evaluation protocol of any kind. If the LSTM line is ever revisited, it needs the peer-reviewed journal version (Pandit et al. 2025, above) or a source with an explicit leave-one-region-out protocol -- not this abstract.
findings.worksAtUngaugedPin: NO, and this source's own mechanism says why: it attributes low western scores to sensor absence. An arbitrary Iowa pin has no sensor by definition.

findings.claim: UNVERIFIED (tier 3, use as lead only): the head-to-head EA-LSTM-vs-XGBoost basin-count ablation this angle asked for may exist in Gauch et al., 'The Proper Care and Feeding of CAMELS: How Limited Training Data Affects Streamflow Prediction' (arXiv:1911.07249; Environmental Modelling & Software), on the same 531 CAMELS basins. The extracted figures -- which were NEVER adversarially verified and must NOT be used as the warrant for any recommendation -- report median NSE by (training years, basins) of: 3yr/13 basins XGBoost 0.41 vs EA-LSTM 0.43; 3yr/53 0.48 vs 0.56; 3yr/531 0.57 vs 0.68; 9yr/13 0.54 vs 0.63; 9yr/531 0.66 vs 0.74, with the authors reportedly stating that at three to six years and 13 basins the two 'result in NSE distributions that do not differ significantly (large p-values)' and that 'the effect size d grows with the number of basins, but has no clear relationship to the number of training years.' IF this holds on verification, it is the single most on-point source for this angle: the deep model's advantage would be driven by BASIN COUNT, not record length -- the exact axis on which this project is starved (19 families) and rich (18 years, 160k site-days) -- and at 13 basins the advantage vanishes into statistical noise. TWO INDEPENDENT REASONS IT STILL WOULD NOT JUSTIFY A PIVOT even if verified: the target is STREAMFLOW, not a water-quality concentration; and the protocol is reportedly temporal-holdout at gauged basins ('we perform temporal validation'), so its numbers are not comparable to our LOFO 0.820. VERIFYING THIS SOURCE IS THE HIGHEST-VALUE REMAINING RESEARCH ACTION FOR THIS ANGLE, and it is cheap -- the preprint is free on arXiv.
findings.effectSize: UNVERIFIED. Reported as EA-LSTM minus XGBoost median NSE: +0.02 at 13 basins/3yr, +0.08 at 53 basins/3yr, +0.11 at 531 basins/3yr, +0.09 at 13 basins/9yr, +0.08 at 531 basins/9yr; significance threshold reportedly Kolmogorov-Smirnov p < 0.01/15 (Bonferroni) AND Cohen's d > 0.35, not met at 13 basins with 3-6 years.
findings.splitProtocol: reported as temporal-holdout at gauged basins (train from Oct 1999 for 3/6/9 years, test Oct 1989 - Sep 1999) -- NOT spatially held out, NOT comparable to our LOFO. Unverified.
findings.nBasins: reported as random subsets of 13, 26, 53, 265, and 531 basins, five random draws at each size below 531. Unverified.
sources: https://arxiv.org/abs/1911.07249 -- TIER 3, NEVER VERIFIED. Free preprint; verification is cheap and should be done before this is cited anywhere.
findings.feasibilityAtN19: If verified, this would be the closest thing in the literature to a direct answer at our scale, and the answer would be that at ~13 basins XGBoost and EA-LSTM are statistically indistinguishable for streamflow -- i.e. no deep-model advantage exists in our regime even on the target where deep models are strongest. Until verified, this must not be used as the warrant for that conclusion; the conclusion is independently supported by the verified Kratzert/Gauch 2024 scaling and subsetting results above.
findings.worksAtUngaugedPin: NO -- the reported protocol is temporal validation at basins the model trained on, which is the level-memorization-permitting regime our deployment target explicitly excludes.

findings.claim: UNVERIFIED (tier 3, use as lead only): the most target-matched pooling experiment in the corpus reportedly found that POOLING SITES HURT for stream nitrate, the opposite of the streamflow finding. Gorski et al. (2024, WRR, doi:10.1029/2023WR036591) reportedly trained LSTMs on 46 predominantly agricultural US sites and found 46 single-site models at median KGE 0.66, 5 attribute-based cluster models at median KGE 0.66, and a single global model on all 46 sites at median KGE 0.63, with the authors reportedly writing 'Developing a single model for all sites reduced performance at several locations with distinct characteristics, suggesting that there is a threshold of dissimilarity beyond which more data does not improve the model,' and elsewhere explicitly denying transfer of the streamflow result: 'While many deep learning studies have shown that national or even global models can outperform local models, it is not clear that this is true for water quality constituents.' THIS CONTRADICTS the verified Kratzert/Gauch 2024 pooling result, and the contradiction is informative rather than fatal: the verified result is STREAMFLOW, the unverified one is NITRATE, and the whole point of this angle is that the two targets may not behave alike. Because Gorski is tier 3 and Kratzert/Gauch 2024 is tier 1, the verified claim wins where they overlap -- but they do not overlap on target, so the honest reading is that the streamflow pooling evidence should not be assumed to carry to nitrate in either direction. THREE DISQUALIFYING CAVEATS reported for Gorski, all unverified: the protocol is temporal-holdout with all 46 sites in training in every scheme (so it contains NO ungauged-basin experiment at all); daily discharge is a REQUIRED model input and is reportedly the top-ranked driver of model performance, which our arbitrary pin does not have; and the paper reportedly contains no RF/XGBoost/GBDT baseline anywhere.
findings.effectSize: UNVERIFIED. Reported as global median KGE 0.63 vs single-site 0.66 vs cluster 0.66 -- a pooling cost of ~0.03 KGE concentrated at distinctive sites.
findings.splitProtocol: reported as temporal-holdout; the companion USGS data release's FGDC dictionary reportedly defines the split variable as a training/validation/prediction TIME PERIOD label. If accurate, none of its KGE values are comparable to a leave-one-basin-out number. Unverified.
findings.nBasins: reported as 46 sites, grouped into 5 attribute clusters or 8 glacial hydrogeologic 'hydro terranes.' Unverified.
sources: https://www.sciencebase.gov/catalog/item/661436d1d34e633466530330 -- companion USGS data release, TIER 3, NEVER VERIFIED.
findings.feasibilityAtN19: The reported grouping design is the most structurally analogous thing found: 46 sites collapsed to 5 or 8 groups is close in spirit to our 85 sites collapsed to 19 families, and if verified it would be a template for how a peer-reviewed nitrate study handled a comparable sample-size constraint. That design relevance is the legitimate tier-3 use of this source.
findings.worksAtUngaugedPin: NO on two counts, if the reports are accurate: no site is ever held out spatially, and daily discharge is a required input unavailable at an ungauged pin. Do not cite the 0.63-0.66 KGE range as achievable by any weather-and-land-use-only model.

findings.claim: UNVERIFIED (tier 3, use as lead only): the anchor PUB result this angle was asked to retrieve -- Kratzert, Klotz, Herrnegger, Sampson, Hochreiter & Nearing (2019), 'Toward Improved Predictions in Ungauged Basins: Exploiting the Power of Machine Learning,' WRR 55(12):11344-11354, doi:10.1029/2019WR026065 -- was NEVER adversarially verified in this corpus. Reported: an out-of-sample 10-member 'PUB LSTM' ensemble achieved median NSE 0.69 over 531 CAMELS catchments versus 0.64 for SAC-SMA calibrated separately in each basin and 0.58 for the NOAA National Water Model, winning in 307/531 (58%) and 347/531 (66%) catchments respectively. FOUR REASONS THIS CANNOT CARRY THE ANGLE even if every number verifies: (a) the target is daily STREAMFLOW, not any water-quality or concentration variable; (b) NO machine-learning baseline of any kind was run -- both benchmarks are process-based models, so the paper provides zero evidence that LSTM beats a booster; (c) the spatial holdout is reportedly a RANDOM k=12-fold split ('splits the 531 basins randomly into k = 12 groups of approximately equal size'), NOT leave-one-region-out and NOT nesting-aware, so every held-out basin retains ~487 training basins including geographically and climatically adjacent ones -- a materially WEAKER transfer test than our LOFO, and the paper reportedly contains no region-blocked variant and no analysis of skill versus distance from the nearest training basin; (d) there is reportedly NO ablation of performance versus number of training basins anywhere in it, every configuration using ~487 or all 531 basins, so it says nothing about n=19.
findings.effectSize: UNVERIFIED. Reported as median NSE 0.69 (LSTM, ungauged) vs 0.64 (SAC-SMA, gauged and locally calibrated) vs 0.58 (NWM) -- +0.05 over the best benchmark.
findings.splitProtocol: reported as spatial-holdout, k=12 RANDOM basin folds (~44 test / ~487 train per fold). This is a genuine spatial holdout but is weaker than leave-one-region-out and weaker than our basin-family LOFO. Unverified.
findings.nBasins: reported as 531 CAMELS catchments (4-2,000 km2, ~30 yr daily), ~28x our 19 independent basin families. Unverified.
sources: https://eartharxiv.org/repository/object/713/download/1565/ -- free preprint copy; verification is cheap.
findings.feasibilityAtN19: NOT FEASIBLE. The reported evidence base is ~28x our independent-unit count with no reduced-n experiment. Two further reported details compound the problem at small n: a heavy left tail the median conceals (mean NSE 0.54 vs median 0.69, minimum -13.02, with SAC-SMA outperforming the transferred LSTM specifically in the low-NSE catchments), and severe seed instability -- 103 of 531 basins reportedly had at least one of 10 ensemble members score NSE < 0, leading the authors to conclude that 'a substantial portion of the uncertainty in these LSTM models is due to randomness, rather than to systematic model structural error.' With only 19 held-out families, per-fold seed variance would likely swamp any effect being measured, so a single-seed LSTM-vs-XGBoost comparison at our scale would be uninterpretable.
findings.worksAtUngaugedPin: The protocol is right in kind -- predictions are made in basins supplying zero training data -- but the target is streamflow and there is no tree baseline, so it predicts nothing about whether an LSTM would beat our booster on nitrate.

findings.claim: UNVERIFIED (tier 3, use as lead only) BUT DIRECTLY ON THE PROJECT'S CORE DIAGNOSIS: multiple independent reports in the corpus converge on the conclusion that STATIC CATCHMENT ATTRIBUTES, NOT TEMPORAL DYNAMICS, carry the cross-site transferable signal in deep hydrologic models -- the same conclusion this project reached empirically from seven failed temporal ablations. (a) Kratzert et al. 2019 reportedly found two LSTMs trained on all 531 basins with identical meteorological forcings, differing only in whether 27 static CAMELS attributes were appended, scored median NSE 0.74 WITH statics vs 0.63 WITHOUT (+0.11, reportedly significant at p < 1e-9) -- while the penalty for never having seen the basin at all was only -0.05 (0.74 in-sample -> 0.69 ungauged). Most of the achievable skill survives never having seen the site; the transferable information lives in the static descriptors. (b) A stream-temperature PUB study (arXiv:2410.19865) reportedly found that starting from a meteorology-only model at median per-site RMSE 1.78C, adding 274 GAGES-II static attributes dropped it to 1.47C while adding river DISCHARGE instead dropped it only to 1.57C, with combined permutation importance of 1.12C for all static attributes versus 0.36C for all discharge features -- and, critically for our feature budget, that just 21 EXPERT-SELECTED attributes were statistically equivalent to all 274 (median RMSE 1.46C vs 1.43C) and actually better on the warmest 10% of observations. IMPLICATION, which rests on the verified Pandit Shapley finding above rather than on these tier-3 numbers: static-attribute enrichment is the higher-value lever than any sequence architecture, and roughly 20 well-chosen static attributes suffice -- a target that is tractable at n=19 in a way that a 256-dimensional learned embedding fit on 531 basins is not.
findings.effectSize: UNVERIFIED. Reported: +0.11 median NSE from static attributes (0.63 -> 0.74), only -0.05 penalty for going ungauged (0.74 -> 0.69); stream temperature meteo-only 1.78C -> +statics 1.47C vs +discharge 1.57C; 21 curated attributes 1.46C vs 274 attributes 1.43C.
findings.splitProtocol: MIXED AND MUST NOT BE CONFLATED. The reported 0.63 and 0.74 statics-vs-no-statics numbers are TEMPORAL-holdout on in-sample basins (train 1981-1995, test 1996-2010) and are NOT spatially held out; only the 0.69 PUB figure is spatial. The stream-temperature numbers are reportedly site-disjoint spatial holdout, but with the split assigned by RECORD LENGTH (782 sites with >=5 yr trained, 580 sites with 1-5 yr tested), so test sites are geographically interspersed with training sites, with no region-level separation and no control for basin nesting -- weaker than our LOFO.
findings.nBasins: reported as 531 (Kratzert 2019) and 782 train / 580 test of 1362 total sites (stream temperature). Both far above n=19.
findings.feasibilityAtN19: The DIRECTION is feasible and is what this angle should hand off: enrich static between-site attributes, keep the booster. The specific mechanisms are not -- a learned R^256 static embedding fit on 531 basins is very unlikely to be identifiable from 19 families, and the '21 expert attributes beat 274' result, if it holds, argues for a hand-curated static set over any learned encoder at our scale.
findings.worksAtUngaugedPin: YES for static attributes -- they are computed from the delineated basin polygon and require no local observations. NO for the discharge input that appears alongside them in the stream-temperature study.

findings.claim: UNVERIFIED (tier 3, use as lead only) -- ON THE 'CHEAPER MIDDLE GROUND' THE ASSIGNMENT ASKED ABOUT (multi-task / shared-embedding models, site embeddings, per-site random effects on top of the existing booster): the corpus produced NO study that evaluates any of these against a gradient-boosted baseline for a water-quality target under spatial holdout. The nearest reported evidence is discouraging and indirect: (a) the Willard et al. (2025) survey reportedly describes the accessible version of entity-aware modeling as direct concatenation of static site characteristics to dynamic inputs -- which 'does not require novel ML architecture and is therefore very accessible,' and which OUR BOOSTER ALREADY DOES -- while a learned ENCODING of those same statics reportedly gave only a 'slight improvement over the static and dynamic concatenation approach' (Tayal et al., lake temperature), with no numeric gain reported; (b) the stream-temperature PUB study reportedly tested regional FINE-TUNING of a large top-down model, the standard remedy for small regional samples, and found it 'yielded performance that mirrored the top-down model very closely,' adding essentially nothing and failing to recover the deficit of small-sample regional models -- though it tested fine-tuning specifically, not embeddings or random effects, which it does not evaluate at all. PREDICTED EFFECT OF ADDING A SITE-EMBEDDING OR RANDOM-EFFECTS LAYER TO OUR BOOSTER: small, and unsupported by any numeric evidence in either tier. A further structural objection applies independently of the evidence: a per-site random effect or site embedding is by construction UNIDENTIFIABLE at a new site, since a fresh map pin has no observations from which to estimate its own effect. Such a layer could improve in-sample fit and would improve nothing at the deployment target unless the effect is itself made a function of static basin attributes -- at which point it is simply the static-attribute enrichment recommended above, wearing a different name.
findings.effectSize: No effect size exists in either tier. The survey reportedly attaches no metric, split protocol, or site count to its encoded-statics comparison; the fine-tuning result is reportedly unquantified in the main text.
findings.splitProtocol: unknown for the survey's encoded-statics claim; reportedly site-disjoint spatial holdout for the fine-tuning experiment.
findings.nBasins: unknown for the survey claim; reportedly 782 train / 580 test for the fine-tuning experiment -- and note that the fine-tuning null result was obtained at LARGE n, so it does not directly bound behavior at n=19.
sources: https://arxiv.org/html/2308.09766v2 -- Willard et al. survey, TIER 3, NEVER VERIFIED.
findings.feasibilityAtN19: Site embeddings and per-site random effects are CHEAP to implement at n=19 but are the wrong target: with 19 independent units, a per-family effect is estimated from ~1 unit of information per parameter and will not generalize. The identifiability objection above is decisive and does not depend on any literature.
findings.worksAtUngaugedPin: NO for any per-site parameter estimated from that site's own observations -- the deployment target has none by definition. Only a mapping from static basin attributes to level works at an arbitrary pin, which is the recommendation already made in findings 2 and 9.

findings.claim: UNVERIFIED (tier 3, use as lead only) -- ON WHETHER GAINS PERSIST UNDER LEAVE-ONE-REGION-OUT, the question the assignment specifically asked. No verified source answers it. The reported tier-3 evidence, where it exists, is that deep-model advantage DEGRADES sharply as the held-out region's training sample shrinks: a stream-temperature PUB study reportedly states 'the grouped models do quite poorly in all regions with less than 15 training sites' and 'when only a few sites are available for training... the models are not seeing sufficient data and site diversity in these cases to be able to extrapolate to unseen locations,' with the worst cases being Lower Colorado (2 training sites, regional LSTM median RMSE 6.38C vs 2.10C for the CONUS model, 3.0x worse) and Souris-Red-Rainy (regional 9.09C, cluster 8.70C), while regions where regional models were competitive were far larger (Pacific Northwest, 142 training sites, regional 1.27C vs CONUS 1.22C). The Willard survey reportedly reports the same pattern for stream temperature -- regional models worse than the CONUS model in 15 of 17 regions -- and describes a 'data synergy' effect in which deep models 'perform better when fed a diverse training dataset spanning multiple regions as opposed to homogeneous dataset on a single region EVEN WHEN the homogeneous data is more relevant to the testing dataset.' A single-state, 19-independent-family Iowa dataset is exactly the homogeneous small-n regime these reports identify as the failure mode. NOTE THAT ALL OF THIS IS STREAM TEMPERATURE, a smoothly-varying, strongly seasonally-forced target dominated by the WITHIN-site signal that our model already handles well (within_r2 0.42, macro_auc 0.90) -- it is not evidence about recovering the BETWEEN-site absolute level of a threshold-exceedance target.
findings.effectSize: UNVERIFIED. Reported: regional LSTM 6.38C vs CONUS 2.10C at 2 training sites; regional 1.27C vs CONUS 1.22C at 142 training sites; regional worse than global in 15/17 regions (magnitude unquantified in the survey).
findings.splitProtocol: reported as spatial-holdout, site-disjoint, with regional models trained on a region's sites and tested on other held-out sites within that same region. Not region-BLOCKED in the sense our LOFO is, and with no control for basin nesting.
findings.nBasins: reported failing regions had 2-15 training sites; succeeding regions had 47-183.
findings.feasibilityAtN19: If these reports verify, our 19 independent basin families sit BELOW the ~15-site threshold at which grouped deep models were observed to fail catastrophically, and roughly an order of magnitude below the region size where a regional deep model was merely competitive. The reported advantage is an effect of large-sample site diversity, not of architecture.
findings.worksAtUngaugedPin: The protocol is site-disjoint and therefore right in kind, but the target is stream temperature, not a nutrient concentration, and the finding is a warning about small regional samples rather than a transferable method.

datasets.name: AgTile-US -- 30 m modeled tile-drainage map of the conterminous United States (Valayamkunnath, Barlage, Chen, Gochis & Franz, 2020)
datasets.years: Single static epoch, approximately 2017 (built from the USDA 2017 Census of Agriculture county tile-drainage statistics, NLCD 2016 cropland, SSURGO soil drainage class, and SRTM slope)
datasets.access: Free public download from Figshare, no authentication, no API required. GeoTIFF and NetCDF. Bulk download only.
datasets.license: Figshare deposit; verify the specific license on the record before redistribution (Scientific Data data descriptors are typically CC-BY, but the deposit terms must be checked). Free for research use.
datasets.coversMultiState: YES -- full conterminous US coverage. This is the property that matters most here: it covers all of Iowa AND the out-of-state portions of the largest multi-state basins, which is exactly where the project's current inner-join under-counting of crop area and N surplus is worst. Unlike the Iowa-clipped CDL/surplus layers, aggregating AgTile-US introduces no new coverage bias for large basins.
datasets.whyUseful: Tile drainage is the control this project already identified as dominant in Iowa hydrology, absent from the 68-feature set, and with no data source identified. The VERIFIED Pandit et al. 2025 Shapley result independently names tile drainage as the leading SPATIAL driver of MEAN nitrate concentration -- i.e. of exactly the between-site term where essentially all remaining headroom lies -- with non-linear thresholds in its influence. That finding also proves a CONUS-extent tile-drainage layer exists and is operationally usable, since Pandit et al. used one. AgTile-US is the leading candidate for that layer.
datasets.howToIncorporate: Create tile_drained_frac_<bucket> for each of the existing 3 distance buckets: rasterize the delineated upstream basin polygon, intersect with the 30 m AgTile-US binary raster, and compute the fraction of basin cells in each distance bucket that are flagged tile-drained -- i.e. exactly the aggregation already used for the 8 CDL crop-class features, on the same grid, so this reuses the existing basin-cell pipeline with no new machinery. Add one basin-wide tile_drained_frac_total as well, since the Shapley result is about the site-level MEAN and the total is the natural between-site scalar. Because the layer is static, it carries no risk of repeating the N-surplus temporal-broadcast failure (-0.166) -- it is a genuine static geographic attribute, the only feature class that has produced wins on this project. Evaluate specifically on between_r2 / between_rate_r2, not on overall LOFO AUC, since the predicted effect is on site ranking. Note the aggregation must use a LEFT join against basin cells with explicit no-data handling, not the inner join that currently under-counts multi-state basins.
datasets.limitations: UNVERIFIED PROVENANCE AND SPECIFICATIONS: every operational detail above (30 m, binary, the four input products, GeoTIFF/NetCDF, Figshare hosting, and the reported 86.03% CONUS / 82.7-93.6% Midwest validation accuracy against 16,000 ground-truth points) comes from a TIER 3 claim that was never adversarially verified. Confirm the record directly before building against it. Substantively: it is a MODELED product, not observed drainage infrastructure, and is derived partly from county-level census statistics, so within-county spatial detail is interpolated rather than measured -- meaning between-basin contrast within a single county may be largely artifactual. It is a single static epoch with no time dimension, so it cannot capture drainage expansion over the 2008-2026 record. And it is binary presence/absence, not drainage DENSITY or intensity, which is the quantity the project's notes actually identify as the dominant control. CROSS-CHECK ACTION: when the PMC embargo on Pandit et al. lifts on 2026-08-09 (https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC12425153/), read the data-availability statement to confirm which tile-drainage layer they actually used -- if it is not AgTile-US, use theirs instead, since theirs is the one with a demonstrated Shapley signal on nitrate.

datasets.name: Pandit et al. 2025 full text and data-availability statement (PubMed Central deposit PMC12425153)
datasets.years: Publication 2025-08-09; PMC deposit becomes free full text on 2026-08-09
datasets.access: Free once the embargo lifts. Currently: Wiley returns HTTP 402/403 to all automated routes, the PMC page returns 403 with 'This article will be available in PMC on August 09, 2026,' Europe PMC lists it as subscription-required with no full-text XML, and NCBI efetch returns front matter only. No preprint exists in any repository. An alternative route available NOW is emailing the corresponding author (Admin Husic, husic@vt.edu), which is within the project's stated acquisition constraint of 'data obtainable by a reasonable request.'
datasets.license: CC-BY-NC (gold open access at the publisher, notwithstanding the access blocks)
datasets.coversMultiState: YES -- CONUS-wide model, with the Mississippi River Basin as the featured application region, so its attribute sources necessarily cover the multi-state portions of Iowa basins.
datasets.whyUseful: This is the single highest-value pending acquisition for the between-site problem. Three specific items are behind the embargo: (1) the DATA-AVAILABILITY STATEMENT naming the exact tile-drainage, road-density, and wetland-cover layers whose Shapley importance is the verified headline -- i.e. the operational provenance for three static attributes that are all absent from our feature set; (2) the reported non-linear THRESHOLD values for those drivers, which would tell us where in the covariate range the effect lives and would inform binning; (3) the Methods section, which would settle whether the spatial-validation folds were nesting-aware (currently unknown, and the reason its protocol cannot be called leak-safe-equivalent to our LOFO), what the site count actually is, and whether discharge was used as a dynamic input -- the last of which determines whether even its KGE 0.34 is attainable by a weather-and-land-use-only model.
datasets.howToIncorporate: Not a feature source directly -- it is the provenance document for finding 2's three recommended features. On or after 2026-08-09, fetch the full text, extract the data-availability statement, and use the named layers (rather than guessed substitutes such as AgTile-US) as the sources for tile_drained_frac_<bucket>, wetland_frac_<bucket>, and road_density_<bucket>, aggregated over basin cells in the existing 3 distance buckets exactly as the CDL crop-class features are. Also extract the site count to replace the currently unverified 95/148 figures, and check the Methods for whether nested sites were grouped in the spatial folds.
datasets.limitations: Embargoed until 2026-08-09 -- approximately 3 weeks from the date of this synthesis, so this is a near-term action rather than a blocked one. Its catchment attributes are reportedly drawn from CAMELS and GAGES-II, which are gauge-referenced products; whether those attributes are computable at an ARBITRARY NLDI-delineated pin (as opposed to at a pre-existing gauged catchment) must be checked, because GAGES-II is distributed as a fixed catalogue of gauged basins, not as a raster stack. If the attributes turn out to be gauge-catalogue lookups rather than rasters, they do NOT work at our deployment target and the underlying national raster layers must be sourced separately.

datasets.name: GAGES-II static catchment attribute set (referenced as an attribute source in tier-3 material)
datasets.resolution: Basin-aggregated attributes, one record per gauged basin -- NOT a raster
datasets.access: Free, public, bulk download from USGS, no authentication
datasets.coversMultiState: CONUS-wide in extent, but see the disqualifying limitation below
datasets.whyUseful: Tier-3 material reports it as the static-attribute source in both the stream-temperature PUB study and (via CAMELS/GAGES-II) the Pandit nitrate model, and reports that a curated ~21-attribute subset was statistically equivalent to the full 274 attributes -- which would be a useful shortlist for what static attributes actually matter for between-site transfer, at a feature count tractable at n=19. Listed here as a SHORTLIST SOURCE for which attributes to pursue, not as a directly ingestible dataset.
datasets.howToIncorporate: Do NOT ingest GAGES-II directly. Use its attribute LIST -- specifically the reported top performers PCT_SLOPE and DRAIN_SQKM, and the reported 'Major Dams' category -- as a shortlist, then source each shortlisted attribute from its underlying national RASTER or vector product so it can be recomputed over an arbitrary NLDI-delineated basin and aggregated to the existing distance buckets. Note the project already carries log_basin_area, so DRAIN_SQKM is redundant; percent slope from a national DEM is the cheap net-new addition.
datasets.limitations: DISQUALIFYING FOR DIRECT USE AT THE DEPLOYMENT TARGET: GAGES-II is a fixed CATALOGUE of pre-delineated gauged basins, keyed to USGS gauge IDs. An arbitrary Iowa map pin is not in the catalogue, so no GAGES-II record exists for it, and there is no lookup that works at the deployment target. Any attribute wanted must be recomputed from its source raster over the NLDI-delineated basin. Additionally, all quantitative claims about GAGES-II attribute importance in this corpus are TIER 3 and were never verified, and they come from a STREAM TEMPERATURE study, not a nutrient one -- attribute rankings are not transferable across targets. Also note the ~2011 vintage: several attributes predate the project's 2008-2026 record midpoint.

refuted.refutedClaim: That the temporal-to-spatial KGE degradation in Pandit et al. 2025 was strongly TARGET-DEPENDENT across streamflow (0.78 -> 0.65), nitrate YIELD (0.59 -> 0.32), and nitrate CONCENTRATION (0.60 -> 0.18), establishing that concentration degrades ~3x more than discharge under spatial holdout.
refuted.whatVerifiersEstablished: Four of the six numbers could not be substantiated in any accessible text, and the load-bearing inference rests entirely on those four. Only the concentration row (0.60 -> 0.18) is verbatim correct. Every retrievable description of the paper frames it as a SINGLE-TARGET model -- 'an LSTM model... to predict daily nitrate concentrations' -- with nitrate yield appearing only as a DERIVED quantity in the 1980-2022 mass-balance analysis, never as a separately validated prediction target with its own KGE. The purported yield figure of 0.32 is suspiciously adjacent to a real number in the abstract, the MRB-subset spatial CONCENTRATION KGE of 0.34, which is the signature of a garbled paraphrase: a real figure re-labeled as a different target. Verifiers also noted a methodological objection that holds even if the missing numbers exist -- comparing raw KGE drops across streamflow and concentration is not a clean measure of transferability difficulty, because KGE bundles correlation, a variance ratio and a mean-bias ratio, and streamflow is far more seasonally forced and autocorrelated than concentration with different signal-to-noise and dynamic range. A ratio of KGE drops across targets is not an effect size.
refuted.whatSurvives: Nothing usable beyond the concentration row already captured in finding 1. DO NOT cite 'concentration transfers ~3x worse than discharge' -- the comparison has no verified basis.

refuted.refutedClaim: That Pandit et al.'s spatial validation was an explicit twelve-fold cross-validation excluding ~8.3% of SITES per fold with their full time series used for validation, and was therefore 'leak-safe in the same sense as our LOFO' and protocol-comparable to our LOFO AUC 0.820 in kind.
refuted.whatVerifiersEstablished: This is the most instructive refutation in the set, because a verifier found affirmative counter-evidence rather than merely failing to confirm. The authors' own results repository (github.com/aayushpandit/EPA-CONUS-Nitrate-LSTM) stores all cross-validation output under a FIVE-fold directory structure, not twelve. More decisively: the verifier downloaded the k-fold metrics artifact (95 stations) and computed median KGE = 0.59 -- which reproduces the paper's 0.60 TEMPORAL validation headline, the number the abstract explicitly DISTINGUISHES from the unmonitored-basin result. So the k-fold procedure the claim describes produced the in-network temporal number, not the ungauged-basin number; the claim attached a spatial-holdout label to the wrong result. The '~8.3%' figure is simply 1/12 and reads as back-derived from an assumed fold count rather than quoted. Separately, on the equivalence assertion: our LOFO exists precisely because splitting by SITE is insufficient in Iowa, since nesting basins share the same upstream water, which is why 85 sites collapse to 19 families. Nothing in the repository, abstract, or the single indexed methods sentence indicates sites were grouped by basin nesting or by overlapping record period. Nested nitrate sensors are pervasive in the MRB, so a per-site split plausibly leaves a held-out site with a nested relative in training -- exactly the leak family-grouping removes.
refuted.whatSurvives: The weaker underlying fact IS corroborated and is retained in finding 1: the study ran a genuine spatial validation in which whole sites were excluded from training, distinct from and much worse than its temporal validation. An indexed sentence from the publisher page reads 'Temporal and spatial cross-validation (CV) were conducted to assess the respective ability of the LSTM models to (1) forecast unseen conditions at sites included in training and (2) make predictions at (pseudo)-unmonitored basins not included in training.' What does NOT survive is the fold count, the per-fold fraction, the full-time-series detail, and above all the leak-safety equivalence to our LOFO.
refuted.lessonForThisProject: Do not treat any external 'spatial holdout' as equivalent to our basin-family LOFO without confirming that nested and temporally-overlapping basins were forced into the same fold. Most published spatial splits mask individual sites, not families, and are therefore weaker transfer tests than ours. This applies equally to the Kratzert 2019 PUB result, whose reported random k=12 site split has the same weakness.

refuted.refutedClaim: That the MRB improvement (spatial KGE 0.18 -> 0.34) is direct evidence that transfer performance improves when the TRAINING POOL is restricted to hydroclimatically similar basins, supporting a regionally-specialized model over a continental one for an Iowa-only product.
refuted.whatVerifiersEstablished: The refutation is a clean conflation of subsetting the EVALUATION set with restricting the TRAINING pool, and it matters because the claim as written would have endorsed the status quo and discouraged the one intervention that could actually add independent between-site units. The abstract describes ONE model -- 'a long short-term memory (LSTM) model using high-frequency sensor data from across the conterminous US' -- and then 'the model's targeted application to the MRB': definite article, singular, the same CONUS-trained model. The 0.34 is the MRB SUBSET of the held-out folds of the CONUS-trained model, not a separately trained MRB-only model. No ablation varying the training pool (CONUS-trained vs MRB-trained, evaluated on the same MRB holdouts) is reported anywhere accessible, and that is the experiment the claim requires. Two confounds explain the 0.18 -> 0.34 gap without any regional-specialization mechanism, and both are properties of the evaluation set: US high-frequency nitrate sensors are overwhelmingly concentrated in the Corn Belt/MRB, so MRB holdout basins have far more near-neighbour training basins (a coverage effect); and MRB nitrate has large-amplitude, strongly seasonal signals, which mechanically inflates KGE relative to low-variance basins elsewhere.
refuted.whatSurvives: The numbers survive and are used in finding 1. What is reversed is the DIRECTION OF THE RECOMMENDATION. The paper's actual workflow -- train on the largest available pool, then apply regionally -- argues for ENLARGING the training pool beyond Iowa while targeting Iowa at inference. This is independently reinforced by the VERIFIED Kratzert/Gauch 2024 subsetting result that models trained on HUC-sized subsets underperform the full pool. Note also that this project is ALREADY at the maximally regionally-specialized end of the axis the refuted claim recommended moving along: our model is Iowa-only by construction, so the claim offered no headroom, only endorsement of a move already made.
refuted.actionableConsequence: The one live structural lever this refutation exposes is pulling in out-of-state nitrate monitoring sites across the MRB to raise the count of independent basin families above 19. That attacks the binding constraint directly, in a way no architecture change does. Whether enough public out-of-state high-frequency nitrate sites exist, and whether their basins are independent of our existing 19 families, is NOT answered anywhere in this angle's evidence and is flagged in 'uncovered'.

refuted.refutedClaim: That Pandit et al. used random forests as an INTERPRETABILITY tool rather than as a competing predictor, quoting the paper as having 'developed interpretable random forest models that explain the spatial variation in long-term streamflow, nitrate concentration, and nitrate yield at 95 sites used for model training,' and that the paper's split protocol is therefore 'not-applicable.'
refuted.whatVerifiersEstablished: The quoted sentence is not in the paper. The strings 'random forest,' 'streamflow,' and 'nitrate yield at 95 sites' appear nowhere in the verified abstract, and 'random forest,' 'XGBoost,' and 'gradient boosting' appear in no accessible metadata for the DOI. One verifier enumerated all 46 OpenAlex-indexed works by Husic and all 15 by Pandit and found none matching the description, and multiple abstract searches for the quoted phrasing returned zero hits. The paper's core characterization was also backwards: it is an LSTM PREDICTION paper whose interpretability layer is SHAPLEY VALUES applied to the deep model, not a random forest. Most consequentially, the claimed protocol of 'not-applicable' is false in the most damaging possible direction -- spatial holdout is the paper's CENTRAL methodological contribution, reported quantitatively in the abstract, and declaring it not-applicable discarded the single most decision-relevant fact this paper offers the project.
refuted.whatSurvives: The claim's BOTTOM-LINE ADVICE survives -- do not cite this paper as evidence that LSTM beats gradient-boosted trees for ungauged-basin nitrate -- but for an entirely different reason than the claim gave. It is not that RF was repurposed as an interpretability tool; it is that NO tree-ensemble baseline of any kind appears in the accessible text. There is no deep-vs-tree comparison in this paper to cite, under any protocol. That surviving sliver is captured in finding 3. Caveat: full text is embargoed, so a supplementary benchmark table cannot be formally ruled out.
refuted.lessonForThisProject: This is the corpus's characteristic failure mode in its purest form: the conclusion was right, the stated warrant was fabricated, and the protocol field was not merely wrong but inverted. Any downstream reasoning that took 'protocol: not-applicable' at face value would have discarded the one paper in the corpus that runs the right experiment on the right target.

refuted.refutedClaim: (Correction rather than refutation, applied throughout this synthesis) That the EPA Science Inventory record is 'the paper,' that it covers 95 of 148 sites for training/validation, and that Kratzert/Gauch et al. 2024's split protocol is 'not-applicable.'
refuted.whatVerifiersEstablished: Three factual corrections that materially change how these sources may be used. (1) The EPA record is an AGU 2023 Fall Meeting PRESENTATION record, not a peer-reviewed paper -- no methods, no DOI, no split protocol. This STRENGTHENS the objection to it: the problem is not a missing basin-count ablation but that there is no methodological content to evaluate at all, so it cannot bear inferential weight in either direction. (2) The '95 sites' figure does not appear in the EPA record -- the string is absent. Only 148 sites is verifiable there, making the ratio to our 19 families ~7.8x, not '5-8x.' The 95 figure appears to have been imported from the later peer-reviewed publication and must not be attributed to the EPA record; it is unverified in that source too. (3) Kratzert/Gauch et al. 2024's protocol is not 'not-applicable' -- it is explicitly TEMPORAL holdout at the same gauged basins the model trained on, which makes the paper doubly non-comparable to our LOFO (wrong target variable AND a level-memorization-permitting protocol). Additionally, 'ungauged' DOES appear in that paper's text as motivating prose, so the correct phrasing is 'no ungauged-basin EXPERIMENT,' not that the word is absent -- a careless reader searching for the term could wrongly conclude it contains PUB results.
refuted.whatSurvives: All three source characterizations survive with these corrections applied, and are used in findings 4 and 5 in corrected form.

uncovered: THE CENTRAL QUESTION IS UNANSWERED BY ANY VERIFIED SOURCE. No head-to-head, spatially held-out comparison of LSTM (or entity-aware LSTM, or a hybrid differentiable model) against XGBoost/random forest/any GBDT for a WATER-QUALITY CONCENTRATION target was found in tier 1. The comparison appears not to have been run by anyone. This is reported as an established absence, not as an untested possibility -- but the search was not exhaustive, and the absence is inferred from the sources examined rather than from a systematic review.

AT WHAT NUMBER OF TRAINING BASINS A DEEP-MODEL ADVANTAGE APPEARS -- no VERIFIED source answers this. The only verified scaling evidence (Kratzert/Gauch 2024) reports the curve is still rising at 531 basins, is figure-only with no numeric medians anywhere in the text, tables, or captions, and never states a minimum viable basin count. The one source that reportedly contains an explicit EA-LSTM-vs-XGBoost sweep across 13/26/53/265/531 basins -- Gauch et al., 'The Proper Care and Feeding of CAMELS' (arXiv:1911.07249) -- IS TIER 3 AND WAS NEVER VERIFIED. Verifying it is the cheapest high-value action remaining for this angle: the preprint is free on arXiv, and if its reported figures hold, it directly answers the assignment's second question.

WHETHER ANY LSTM PUB GAIN PERSISTS UNDER LEAVE-ONE-REGION-OUT -- unanswered by any verified source, and this was explicitly asked. No verified paper reports a region-blocked variant, and none reports skill as a function of the held-out basin's distance or dissimilarity from the nearest training basin. The reported spatial holdouts in tier-3 material are RANDOM site splits (Kratzert 2019, k=12 random folds) or record-length splits with geographically interspersed test sites (arXiv:2410.19865) -- both materially weaker transfer tests than our basin-family LOFO. No source in either tier controls for basin nesting the way our CV does.

THE 'CHEAPER MIDDLE GROUND' THE ASSIGNMENT ASKED ABOUT -- multi-task / shared-embedding models, site-embedding regularization, or per-site random effects layered on the existing booster -- HAS NO EVIDENCE IN EITHER TIER evaluated against a GBDT baseline for a water-quality target under spatial holdout. Zero studies. The tier-3 material that touches it is discouraging but indirect (learned static encoders giving only a 'slight improvement' over plain concatenation, which our booster already does; regional fine-tuning adding essentially nothing over a global model) and both are unquantified and from stream temperature. The recommendation in finding 10 therefore rests on a STRUCTURAL identifiability argument rather than on evidence: a per-site effect estimated from a site's own observations is undefined at a fresh map pin, so the only admissible form is a mapping from static basin attributes to level -- which is simply the static-attribute enrichment of finding 2 under another name.

WHETHER PANDIT ET AL.'S LSTM USED DISCHARGE AS A DYNAMIC INPUT. This is not a footnote -- it determines whether even their MRB spatial KGE of 0.34 is attainable by a weather-and-land-use-only model at an ungauged pin. LSTM nitrate-concentration models of this type commonly ingest discharge. Unresolvable until the full text is accessible on 2026-08-09.

THE SITE COUNT AND SPATIAL-FOLD CONSTRUCTION OF PANDIT ET AL. Both the 95 and 148 figures are unverified, the two evaluations may or may not use the same site set, and it is unknown whether nested sites were grouped in the spatial folds. A median KGE computed over an unknown and possibly small number of held-out MRB basins is a fragile statistic with unreported uncertainty. Resolvable on 2026-08-09 via PMC12425153.

POSSIBLE DATA OVERLAP BETWEEN PANDIT ET AL. AND THIS PROJECT'S OWN SITES. Their training data are high-frequency nitrate sensors across the CONUS, which necessarily include USGS and plausibly Iowa IWQIS sensors -- and Iowa's IWQIS network is one of the densest high-frequency nitrate networks in the US. A large share of their sites may literally BE our sites. If so, their result is not independent external validation of our numbers, and their spatial folds may carry the same nesting pseudoreplication our basin-family CV was built to eliminate. Unverifiable without the full text and site list.

WHETHER ENOUGH INDEPENDENT OUT-OF-STATE MRB NITRATE SITES EXIST TO RAISE n ABOVE 19 FAMILIES. This is the one structural lever the refutations exposed -- both the verified Kratzert/Gauch 2024 subsetting result and the corrected reading of Pandit's train-continentally-deploy-regionally workflow point at enlarging the basin pool rather than specializing the model. But NOTHING in this angle's evidence establishes how many public high-frequency or grab-sample nitrate monitoring sites are available outside Iowa in the MRB, what their record lengths are, whether their basins are independent of our existing 19 families, or whether their basin attributes are computable through the same NLDI pipeline. This is the highest-value follow-up question this angle generated and it belongs to a different angle -- it is a data-acquisition question, not an architecture question.

TILE-DRAINAGE DENSITY AS OPPOSED TO PRESENCE. The project's notes identify drainage DENSITY as the dominant control.
